strengths: ReVisiT is a simple, training-free decoding intervention with a clear intuition: reuse cached vision-token representations as reference distributions rather than performing additional model passes.

The evaluation covers three established hallucination benchmarks, two main LVLM families, and an additional MoE model. Reporting recall/coverage alongside hallucination rates helps reveal trivial reductions caused by mentioning fewer objects.
The method generally improves the strongest hallucination metrics over greedy decoding, with especially clear gains for LLaVA on POPE and DeepSeekVL2 on CHAIR.
The paper includes useful component ablations, full POPE results, qualitative examples, and hardware-level latency measurements. The presentation is mostly clear and visually polished.
weaknesses: The method is not reproducibly specified. Equation 8 and Tables 8/10 implement normalized multiplication of probabilities, equivalently addition of log-probabilities, whereas Algorithm 1 multiplies probabilities and then applies another softmax. These operations produce fundamentally different distributions. Exact task-specific alpha values are also omitted despite alpha being selected separately by task, and the DeepSeekVL2 layer/threshold settings are unspecified.

The central mechanistic claim is insufficiently isolated. Because the reference token is selected to minimize divergence from the base distribution and is then multiplied into that distribution, ReVisiT may mainly sharpen existing language-model preferences rather than inject visual evidence. Essential controls—such as shuffled-image tokens, tokens from another image, random vision-token selection, self-reweighting, or matched entropy/temperature sharpening—are absent. The few selected logit-lens examples do not establish the claimed causal mechanism.

Several reported gains are small and uncertainty is not quantified. For Qwen2.5-VL, improvements over greedy are often only a few tenths of a point and results are mixed across recall, coverage, Hal, and Cog. There are no confidence intervals, bootstrap tests, or robustness analyses over sampled CHAIR subsets and hyperparameter selection.

The efficiency claim is incomplete. The approach can require projecting and caching every vision token from many decoder layers over a very large vocabulary, especially for dynamic-resolution Qwen inputs. Per-generated-token latency alone does not clarify whether this one-time projection is included and omits time-to-first-token, end-to-end latency, peak memory, and scaling with image-token count or output length. Thus “negligible overhead” and “memory-efficient” are not adequately demonstrated.

Evaluation is narrowly concentrated on object-hallucination benchmarks. There is no general multimodal-quality or human evaluation showing that the altered decoding preserves fluency, instruction following, reasoning, attributes, and relations. The reduced recall/coverage in some settings reinforces this concern.

The contribution is relevant and promising, but the specification inconsistency, missing exact settings, incomplete efficiency accounting, and lack of mechanism-matched controls prevent a clear finding of soundness and reproducibility in the current version. These appear addressable in a revision, motivating a borderline Findings score rather than rejection on scope or fundamental feasibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP/multimodal problem: reducing LVLM object hallucination without training, external models, or extra decoding passes.

ReVisiT is conceptually simple and potentially useful: cached projections of internal vision-token representations are used to adjust the next-token distribution. Evaluation covers three hallucination benchmarks, two principal LVLMs, and an additional MoE model.
The comparison includes several established inference-time baselines, detailed POPE results, a component ablation, qualitative cases, and measured decoding latency.
weaknesses: The evidence does not establish the central causal claim that visually grounded information from the selected vision token drives the improvements. Because the method selects the reference distribution most similar to the base distribution, it may primarily reinforce or sharpen the model's existing preference. Essential controls—random or shuffled vision tokens/images, mean-token references, alternative selection criteria, and base-distribution sharpening—are absent.

The method is not reproducibly specified. Equation 8 says to multiply two probability distributions and renormalize, whereas Algorithm 1 applies a softmax to their element-wise probability product. The appendix instead describes log-probability fusion and reports values consistent with adding log probabilities. These operations yield materially different distributions.

Task-specific alpha values are not reported, although alpha is selected per task from a six-order-of-magnitude range. The development set and selection criterion are also unspecified. Other consequential details, including normalization before applying the language-model head, are unclear, and no usable code link is provided in the manuscript.

Many gains are small and no statistical uncertainty, bootstrap analysis, or repeated sampling is reported. For example, Qwen's CHAIR-S improvement is only 32.2 to 31.6 on 500 images, while its average POPE accuracy is effectively tied with SID and its F1 is lower. The paper consequently overstates consistent superiority.

The efficiency claim omits an important cost. The stated cache has size |layers| x |vision tokens| x |vocabulary|; with Qwen's large vocabulary, multiple even-numbered layers, and potentially many high-resolution vision tokens, this can require substantial projection computation and memory. Peak memory, cache construction time, and end-to-end latency are not reported, so the claimed negligible overhead and memory efficiency are insufficiently supported.

Evaluation is narrowly centered on object-hallucination metrics. Mixed AMBER results, the lack of broad caption-quality or general multimodal-task evaluation, and only anecdotal open-ended examples leave open whether the method improves overall visual grounding rather than suppressing or distorting useful generation.

The ablation does not isolate the main proposed ingredients—JSD-based token selection and multiplicative fusion. Thus, even accepting the reported numbers, the paper provides inadequate evidence for why ReVisiT works or whether its particular mechanism is necessary.

Overall, the idea is promising but the current submission falls short of Findings-level soundness and reproducibility. Resolving the mathematical inconsistency, fully specifying tuning, adding causal controls and uncertainty estimates, and reporting end-to-end compute and memory costs are important revisions that could reasonably be completed for a subsequent cycle.

strengths: ReVisiT is a simple and practically useful inference-time method: it reuses cached vision-token projections, requires neither training nor an external model, and adds only about 2–3.5% measured latency. The evaluation covers complementary generative and discriminative hallucination benchmarks, two dense LVLMs, and an additional MoE model. Full POPE breakdowns, latency measurements, ablations, and qualitative examples provide broader evidence than a single-benchmark study.

The empirical pattern is generally favorable: ReVisiT reduces CHAIR hallucination rates for both principal models, improves POPE accuracy in every model/setting combination, and remains competitive on AMBER. The gains are particularly convincing for LLaVA on POPE and for DeepSeekVL2 on CHAIR.
The motivation and high-level procedure are clearly presented, and the approach addresses an important NLP/multimodal problem with an appealing efficiency–quality tradeoff.
weaknesses: The evidence does not isolate the claimed mechanism. Because the selected vision-token distribution is explicitly chosen to minimize divergence from the base distribution and then multiplied with it, the method may partly act as base-distribution sharpening. Essential controls—vocabulary constraint alone, shuffled-image or shuffled-vision-token projections, random-token selection, and alternative selection rules—are missing.

No confidence intervals, bootstrap tests, or repeated evaluation samples are reported for task performance. Several central improvements are small—for example, Qwen2.5-VL CHAIRS changes from 32.2 to 31.6 on only 500 CHAIR images—so it is unclear which gains exceed sampling variability.

Reproducibility is weakened by an important mathematical inconsistency. Equation 8 specifies multiplying probabilities and renormalizing, whereas Algorithm 1 applies softmax to the element-wise product of probabilities; Tables 8 and 10 instead appear to add log-probabilities, corresponding to the former rule. These procedures can produce materially different outputs.

The task-specific threshold-selection protocol is underspecified: exact alpha values for each benchmark are not reported, nor is a held-out validation procedure described. Selecting alpha from 10^-1 to 10^-6 directly on benchmark results could introduce test-set tuning, especially when competing methods use default hyperparameters.

The evaluation concentrates on object hallucination and does not quantify general response quality, fluency, instruction following, or non-object grounding. This matters because the no-subset ablation demonstrates severe degeneration and the authors themselves note possible overemphasis of visually salient content.

The claimed memory efficiency is insufficiently analyzed. Caching a |J| × |v| × |V| projection tensor can be large for high-resolution Qwen inputs and many candidate layers; peak memory, preprocessing cost, and scaling with image-token count are not reported. Overall, the work appears sound and useful enough for Findings, but the missing controls, uncertainty analysis, and reproducibility ambiguities limit confidence in a main-conference recommendation.

strengths: The manuscript presents a simple and intuitively motivated training-free decoding method: dynamically restrict the candidate vocabulary, select a vision-token projection close to the current output distribution, and fuse the two distributions. The method is relevant to multimodal NLP and requires no model retraining or auxiliary model.

The evaluation is unusually broad for a decoding paper, covering hallucination-focused and general VQA benchmarks, two principal LVLM families, and an additional CHAIR scalability study involving seven model configurations.

ReVisiT generally improves over greedy decoding. The clearest results include the LLaVA HallusionBench qAcc gain from 11.55 to 20.22, reductions in both CHAIR hallucination metrics, and consistent—albeit often modest—VQAv2 improvements.

The paper includes useful component ablations. The severe failures with full-vocabulary projection, random selection, and maximum-JSD selection demonstrate that vocabulary restriction and minimum-JSD selection are consequential rather than decorative design choices.

The motivation analysis reports sample counts, confidence intervals, a paired nonparametric test, and detailed definitions. The presentation is generally clear, with informative diagrams, extensive appendices, and numerical values accompanying the qualitative examples. weaknesses: The central interpretability claim is stronger than the evidence supports. Restricting a distribution to 176 object words necessarily promotes an object word to top-1 without adding information; the reported 2.03% to 40.44% comparison therefore conflates semantic information with candidate removal. The paper provides no frequency-matched, random-subset, shuffled-image, text-token, or untrained-model control, and no spatial localization test. Because final-layer vision states have already mixed globally through the decoder, the results establish decodable image-level object information, not necessarily intrinsic or localized semantics of individual vision tokens.

The method is not reproducibly specified. Exact task-specific alpha values are omitted, along with how they were selected and on which data; the paper only says that alpha was chosen from 10^-1 to 10^-6. Candidate-layer choices for the five additional model configurations in the scalability experiment are also absent. The VQAv2 split and evaluated sample count are not stated, the 500 sampled COCO image identifiers are not supplied, and the GPT-4 judge version is unspecified. No code or artifact availability is indicated.

Algorithm 1 contradicts Equation 6 and the numerical case studies. Equation 6 and Tables 13/15 multiply probabilities and renormalize, equivalently adding log-probabilities. Algorithm 1 instead forms a probability product and applies softmax to that product, which generally produces a very different, near-uniform distribution. This is a material implementation ambiguity.

Most main-result gains are small and no uncertainty or significance analysis is provided for them. For example, MMMU changes by only 0.74 points on LLaVA and 0.07 on Qwen, while several POPE conditions regress relative to greedy or SID. Results are reported from a single deterministic run and one sampled 500-image CHAIR subset, so the evidence does not establish that the smaller improvements are robust.

The efficiency claim is incomplete and potentially misleading. Caching projections of every vision token from every candidate layer over the full vocabulary has size |J|×|v|×|V|, which can be substantial for Qwen2.5-VL's large vocabulary and resolution-dependent visual-token count. The paper reports only decoding milliseconds per generated token, without peak memory, cache-construction cost, end-to-end latency, output lengths, or scaling with image resolution. Thus the claims of memory efficiency and negligible overall overhead are not adequately supported.

The causal analysis removing all vision tokens places the model in an atypical input condition, and token-level observations within captions are treated as statistical units despite strong within-image dependence. The extremely small Wilcoxon p-values over 88,706 correlated token positions are therefore difficult to interpret; an image-level or clustered analysis would be more appropriate.

Overall, the method is promising and the empirical breadth makes the case close to Findings, but the unsupported interpretability language, missing experimental specifications, pseudocode/equation inconsistency, and incomplete efficiency accounting currently prevent a clear sound-and-reproducible Findings recommendation. These issues appear addressable in a revision rather than requiring fundamental reconstruction.

strengths: ReVisiT is a conceptually simple, training-free decoding intervention that reuses internal vision-token representations and avoids extra model forward passes during autoregressive decoding.
The evaluation covers complementary hallucination, captioning, binary grounding, and general VQA benchmarks, with detailed POPE breakdowns and comparisons to several established decoding baselines.

The paper includes useful diagnostic analyses, ablations over layer choice, vocabulary threshold, and token-selection rule, as well as runtime measurements and experiments across multiple model families and sizes.
The presentation is generally clear, and the appendices document benchmark protocols, qualitative cases, and several intermediate statistics.
weaknesses: The central interpretability claim is not established by the reported constrained-vocabulary experiment. Restricting every projection to a manually chosen list of object synonyms makes an object label inevitable and mechanically increases recall. There is no chance-normalized baseline, shuffled-image test, comparison with text-token states, or other control showing that the recovered label is specifically encoded by the corresponding visual content.

The method lacks a decisive causal control for the vision signal. Min-JSD explicitly selects, from many candidates, the vision-token distribution most similar to the base output and then multiplies the two distributions. This can behave like adaptive sharpening of the language model's existing preference. A mismatched-image reference, non-visual hidden-state reference, or comparable distribution-sharpening baseline is needed to show that the improvements arise from grounded visual semantics rather than selection over a large candidate pool.

The downstream evidence lacks uncertainty estimates or significance tests. Several headline improvements are small—for example, around 0.1 points on some MMMU and POPE comparisons—and CHAIR uses only 500 sampled images. It is therefore unclear which gains are robust rather than sampling or evaluation variation. The HallusionBench results additionally depend on an incompletely specified GPT-4 judge.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper says alpha is selected separately by task from 1e-1 to 1e-6 but does not report the exact value for every benchmark or explain what development data was used. Layer choices are described imprecisely as 'mostly' last-layer or even-layer selection, and configurations for the additional InternVL and larger models are missing. This creates substantial test-set-tuning and replication concerns.

The mathematical specification is internally inconsistent. Equation 6 and the qualitative tables describe multiplication followed by normalization, equivalently addition of log-probabilities. Algorithm 1 instead multiplies already normalized probabilities and then applies another softmax to that product. These operations yield materially different distributions, so the implemented method cannot be reconstructed unambiguously.

The efficiency claim is incomplete. The algorithm caches a tensor of size |J| x |v| x |V|; for Qwen2.5-VL with many visual tokens, a 151k vocabulary, and all even decoder layers, this can require very large memory and substantial first-step projection cost. Only amortized per-token latency is reported, without time-to-first-token, end-to-end latency, peak memory, or a clear accounting of cache construction.

The broad model-agnostic claim is stronger than the evidence: full five-benchmark comparisons are provided for only two 7B models, while the other model sizes and architectures are evaluated only on CHAIR and only against greedy decoding. One configuration even worsens sentence-level CHAIR substantially for LLaVA-1.5-13B.

Overall, the idea is potentially useful, but the missing causal controls, ambiguous algorithm, under-specified tuning, and incomplete efficiency accounting prevent a sound and reproducible Findings recommendation in its current form. These are important but plausibly addressable revisions for a future cycle.

strengths: ReVisiT is a simple, training-free decoding method with an intuitive formulation: construct a context-dependent candidate vocabulary, select a relevant vision-token projection using minimum Jensen-Shannon divergence, and combine it with the base distribution. It requires neither auxiliary models nor additional forward passes.

The evaluation is unusually broad for a decoding paper: five benchmarks covering caption hallucination, binary grounding, general VQA, and multimodal reasoning; detailed comparisons on two distinct LVLM families; and CHAIR results across seven model configurations from three architecture families.

The empirical results are generally positive. The HallusionBench improvement for LLaVA-1.5-7B is substantial, while CHAIR, POPE, MMMU, and VQAv2 show mostly consistent—if sometimes modest—gains. Comparisons against six decoding baselines and the per-benchmark POPE breakdown strengthen the evidence.

The ablations directly test the vocabulary restriction, token-selection rule, layer scope, and threshold. The catastrophic behavior without appropriate restriction also usefully identifies an important operational condition of the method.

The motivation analyses use explicit sample sizes, confidence intervals, paired image-removal comparisons, and a Wilcoxon test. The latency experiment includes warm-up, repeated measurements, hardware details, and variability estimates.
The paper is clearly organized, visually polished, and relevant to current NLP research on grounded multimodal generation.
weaknesses: The evidence for the strong interpretability claim is not sufficiently controlled. The constrained probe must choose among 176 object synonyms, and success means retrieving any ground-truth object anywhere in the image for every vision token. This neither establishes spatial/token-level alignment nor rules out image-level category priors. Shuffled-image controls, random representations, frequency baselines, and region-level localization tests are needed before concluding that individual vision tokens intrinsically encode interpretable object semantics. The full-vocabulary comparison alone is not an adequate control because restricting the candidate space mechanically raises recall.

Reproducibility is incomplete at a consequential point. The threshold alpha is said to be selected separately for each task from 1e-1 to 1e-6, but the final value for each model/benchmark and the held-out selection protocol are not reported. It is therefore unclear whether evaluation sets influenced tuning. Layer pools were also chosen empirically without specifying the development data. Exact prompts and evaluated split/sample size are missing for some evaluations, notably VQAv2.

Algorithm 1 conflicts with the mathematical definition and reported examples. Equation 6 and Tables 13/15 normalize the element-wise product of two probability distributions, whereas Algorithm 1 applies another softmax to that product; these produce very different outputs. The algorithm also says to sample despite all experiments using deterministic greedy decoding. This ambiguity should be corrected.

The efficiency claim is only partly supported. The reported metric is decoding latency per generated token, while the method precomputes and caches a matrix of size |J|×|v|×|V|. For all-layer Qwen settings this may have substantial initialization and memory costs, neither of which is measured. End-to-end latency, peak memory, cache precision, and scaling with image resolution/output length are needed to substantiate the claims of negligible overhead and memory efficiency.

Most main-result gains are small, and no confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-seed/sample analyses are supplied for those results. This matters particularly for the 0.02–1 point differences on MMMU, VQAv2, POPE, and several CHAIR configurations. The broader seven-model experiment compares only against greedy decoding, and LLaVA-1.5-13B actually worsens on sentence-level CHAIR despite the claim of consistent hallucination reduction.

The baseline set omits several closely related decoding-time hallucination methods discussed in the paper, such as HALC, OPERA, and attention-calibration approaches. Coupled with task-specific tuning of ReVisiT and default parameters for competitors, this limits confidence that the reported ranking reflects a uniformly fair comparison.

Overall, the method appears promising and likely sound enough for Findings, but the unsupported strength of the interpretability conclusion, tuning ambiguity, specification inconsistency, and incomplete end-to-end efficiency accounting prevent a confident main-conference recommendation.
